## First, the scope

I read "my financial situation" as the company's P&L in this dataset (orders, revenue, cost, margin). If you meant personal finances, that's outside what these models cover.

## 2023 — the year in governed numbers

| Measure | 2023 | vs 2022 |
|---|---|---|
| kp:TotalSales (net revenue) | **$313.68M** | −28.5% (from $438.52M) |
| kp:TotalCost (COGS) | $138.13M | −28.6% |
| kp:Margin (gross profit) | **$175.55M** | −28.3% |
| kp:MarginPercent | **55.97%** | +0.10pp |
| kp:GrossRevenue (at list) | $333.43M | −28.5% |
| kp:DiscountAmount / kp:DiscountRate | $19.75M / 5.92% | rate flat (5.92% in 2022) |
| kp:OrderCount | 159,695 | −17.6% |
| kp:AverageOrderValue | $1,964.25 | −13.2% |
| kp:AverageSellingPrice | $259.93 | −13.1% |
| kp:UnitsPerOrder / kp:LineCount | 7.56 / 383,837 | flat / −17.7% |

The shape of 2023: a substantial top-line contraction with **completely intact unit economics**. Margin percentage, discount rate, and basket size (units per order) are all flat to slightly better than 2022. executed_malloy:
import "finance.malloy"

run: finance_order -> {
  group_by: yr is DT.year
  aggregate:
    net_revenue
    cost_of_goods_sold
    gross_profit
    gross_margin_percent
    gross_revenue
    discount_amount
    discount_rate
    order_count
    average_selling_price
  where: DT >= @2021-01-01 and DT < @2025-01-01
  order_by: yr
  limit: 10
}
---
import "finance.malloy"

run: finance_order -> {
  group_by: yr is DT.year
  aggregate:
    net_revenue
    gross_profit
    order_count
  where: (DT >= @2023-01-01 and DT < @2023-04-21)
      or (DT >= @2024-01-01 and DT < @2024-04-21)
  order_by: yr
  limit: 10
}
---
import "sales.malloy"

run: sales_performance -> {
  group_by: yr is DT.year
  aggregate: average_order_value, units_per_order, line_count
  where: DT >= @2021-01-01 and DT < @2025-01-01
  order_by: yr
  limit: 10
}
